Negative aqueous PCR does not exclude immune-mediated stromal disease (low yield in stromal-only disease).
2. Acanthamoeba keratitis — Classic cause of a stromal ring and punctate keratitis; less likely because culture/PCR/confocal were reported normal, but still considered if contact-lens use or severe pain is clarified.
3. Contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis (atypical/partially treated) — Can produce ringlike stromal inflammation and AC reaction; negative Gram/culture lowers probability but prior antibiotic use or fastidious organisms can give false-negatives.
4. Fungal keratitis (filamentous) — Can produce stromal infiltrates and immune rings; KOH/culture negative makes this less likely but false-negatives occur early or after therapy.
5. Interstitial keratitis from systemic infection (syphilis, TB) or immune-mediated keratitis — Bilateral stromal inflammation with KPs/uveitis can be due to syphilis or other systemic causes; consider in a bilateral picture and when infectious corneal tests are unrevealing.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis / guide therapy (for ophthalmology):
- Corneal epithelial scraping/biopsy for HSV PCR (from corneal tissue), repeat culture if any epithelial defect.
- Treponemal serology (RPR + treponemal-specific test) and consideration of TB testing if history/exam suggests.
- Re-check contact-lens history and pain severity; consider repeat confocal imaging if Acanthamoeba still suspected.
- Start prompt ophthalmology-guided therapy: consider systemic/topical antiviral therapy and cautious topical corticosteroid under coverage if herpetic stromal keratitis is suspected; avoid empiric steroids without ophthalmology guidance if infection not excluded.
